lawyer:
ABM Golam Majid, Advocate ----- For the appellants. 
Shah Azizur Rahman, AAG with AQ Rashid Ahmed, Advocate ----- For the State.
parties:
Nazrul Islam and others ----- Appellants.
Vs.
The State ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
5. The learned Sessions Judge on consideration of evidence on record found the accused appellants guilty under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment as aforesaid. 

 7. Mr. ABM Golam Mojid the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Sessions Judge had based his conviction of the accused appellants upon so-called confessional statement of accused appellant Nazrul and accused Kashem. He has submitted that there is no independent corroborating evidence whatsoever for finding the accused appellants guilty. So far as the confessional statements of accused appellant Nazrul and accused Kashem are concerned, he submitted, the confessional statements are self-exculpatory and could at best be considered as admission of certain circumstances against the accused appellant Nazrul and accused Kashem who made the confessional statements. Again the confessing accused made the statements under duress as they were made over to the police immediately after the making of their confessional statements. They were under threat that they would be sent back to the police in case they failed to make confessional statements as desired by the police. The learned Advocate for the appellants has stated that the accused Nazrul and Kashem had also retracted their confessional statement soon after making the same. In these circumstances he has submitted that the conviction and sentence of accused appellant Nazrul and accused Kashem cannot be sustained and the conviction of the remaining accused appellants who were involved in their statements by the confessing accused Nazrul and Kashem cannot be sustained also because in the absence of any other evidence against them, confessional statement of a co-accused would amount to no evidence. It is also submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellants that the learned trial Court considered Ext. 4, the inquest report and based his judgment on the same. This was an illegality. The learned Advocate for the appellants further submitted that the medical officer who held post-mortem examination was not examined and cross-examined by the prosecution as required under section 509A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Therefore, the post-mortem report should not be considered by the Court. In this circumstances, the learned Advocate for the appellants has submitted the judgment and order of conviction of the learned Sessions Judge do not deserve to be sustained. 

 9. Before we consider the submission of the learned Advocate for both the sides it is worthwhile to notice the evidence adduced by the prosecution bearing upon the case. 

 17. PW 9 SI Abdus Sattar is the Investigating Officer of the case. He proved his inquest report before the Court as Ext. 4. He has stated that he arrested the accused Nazrul and Kashem on 4.5.85 and they confessed before him to have committed the murder of Sabdul, and then he sent them to the Magistrate for recording their confessional statement On that day he made an application to the Magistrate for taking the confessing accused to his custody on remand. It was suggested to him that he made prayer for remand only to terrorise the confessing accused. It has also been suggested that he had physically tortured the confessing accused to obtain the confessional statements. By cross- examination of this witness certain omissions in the statement of the witnesses before him had been obtained. The accused also adduced the evidence of one DW namely, Rahim Boksh. He has stated that on the night of occurrence at about 8-30 PM he fed Nazrul and 3 other villagers in his own. All of them were cultivators and they were engaged in his house for earth work. After taking meals accused Nazrul and his son Abdur Rahman had together slept in the south bhiti hut. In the morning he woke up and heard that a dead body was found in the field of Molla Kua. They went to the place of occurrence together with Nazrul and Abdur Rahman and saw the dead body of Sabdul. None was aware how Sabdul had met his, death. It appears from his cross-examination that this witness is a cousin of the father of Nazrul and this witness was not summoned. 

 18. These are all about the evidence on behalf of the prosecution and the defence. It is needless to observe that there is no eye-witness of the occurrence, and the case depends on circumstantial evidence and the confessional statement made by accused Nazrul and Kashem. The circumstantial evidence sought to be proved by the prosecution is that the deceased was called away by accused Nazrul at about 8 PM in the night following 21.4.85. But this circumstance has been for the first time put in the mouth of PW 2, and witness onward from the PW 2 have sought to say that they heard from PW 7 Papia, wife of Sabdul, that accused appellant Nazrul had called away her husband on the pretext of gathering honey. This important piece of evidence is found missing both in the FIR and the evidence of the PW 1 Akkas Ali, the elder brother of deceased Sabdul who made the FIR. We get from the evidence of PW 7 that at the place of occurrence many persons gathered including the, elder brother of her husband PW 1 Akkas Ali and PW 2 Kawsar Ali, The FIR must have been lodged after hearing from the PW. 7. There is no reason why the FIR should not contain this important circumstance when that was the only clue available at the time of lodging the First Information Report. Now, although the First Information Report may be sketchy and may omit the details of a case, it is the first case in point of time advanced by the prosecution. The First Information Report is the genesis of the case, when the FIR does not contain an important statement deposed to by the witnesses, it is clear that there has been subsequent embellishment of the prosecution case in the course of trial making the case untrustworthy. This view is supported by the decision in the case of Md. Ali Hyder and others Vs. State, reported in 40 DLR 97 and also the case of Moniruddin Sana @ Mani and others Vs. The State, reported in 40 DLR 402. Therefore the prosecution case that appellant Nazrul had called away Sabdul from his house in the night of occurrence cannot be believed. 

 20. So far as appellant Abdur Sukkur, Shajahan, Moslem Ali are concerned the only material against them is the confessional statement of co-accused Nazrul and Kashem. The confessional statement of co-accused cannot be evidence against non-confessing accused under section 3 of the Evidence Act. The confessing accused made such statement against non-confessing accused in the absence of the latter and this statement is also not tested by cross-examination. Again section 30 of the Evidence Act is to the effect that the court may take into consideration the confessional statement of a co-accused jointly tried against the person who does not confess but section 114(b) of the Evidence Act is to the effect that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in material particulars. All these aspects of confession of a co-accused have weighed with the superior courts to find that conviction of the non-confessing accused cannot be based only upon the confessional statement made by a co-accused. Since against the accused appellants Abdul Sukur, Shajahan and Moslem there is no other evidence or material except the so-called confessional statement of appellant Nazrul and Kashem it can be safely said that the learned trial Court committed illegality in finding them guilty and convicting them as he has done only upon the confessional statement of co-accused. The confessional statement of accused Nazrul cannot also incriminate him in view of the nature of the confessional statement and other circumstances attending it referred to above. Therefore, the conviction and sentence passed upon the accused appellant Nazrul cannot also he sustained.
